title: How the web works
subtitle: Type a URL, press Enter, and a dozen systems cooperate in under a second. Let’s follow one request all the way.

sections.title: URLs and clients/servers
sections.body:
You type an address, press Enter, and a page appears. It feels like magic, but it is a conversation between two parties, and learning to read it is the first step to building for the web. The web is a client–server system: a browser (the client) requests resources from a web server.

Look closely at what you typed. A URL such as https://example.com:443/docs?page=2#top has scheme (protocol), host, port, path, query string and fragment, like a postal address with country, city, street and flat. One quirky detail: the fragment never leaves the browser, so the server never sees it. In https://a.com/x?y=1#z, the part “z” is the fragment, used only by the browser.

choices.text: A fragment used only by the browser.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It is not sent to the server.

keynotes: The web is a client–server system: a browser (client) requests resources from a web server.
A URL such as https://example.com:443/docs?page=2#top has scheme, host, port, path, query string and fragment.
The fragment never leaves the browser.

sections.title: DNS: names to addresses
sections.body:
Computers do not understand “example.com”; they route by IP address. So before anything else, your browser asks DNS, the internet’s phone book, to resolve the host name into a number. Press Enter on a name you have never visited, and a resolver does the legwork.

You will be glad to hear that the answer is cached at several levels (browser, OS, resolver) for its TTL, so repeat visits skip the lookup altogether. The TTL controls how long a cached DNS answer may be reused before it must be asked for again.

choices.text: How long an answer may be cached.

figures.caption: Figure 1.2.1 — DNS lookup
figures.note: The resolver does the legwork and caches the answer.

keynotes: Computers route by IP address, so the browser first asks DNS to resolve the host name.
The answer is cached at several levels (browser, OS, resolver) for its TTL.

sections.title: HTTP request and response
sections.body:
Once the browser knows the address, the two sides talk in a plain-text language called HTTP, and you can learn it in a minute. HTTP is a text protocol: the client sends a request (method, path, headers, optional body); the server answers with a response (status code, headers, body).

The methods are verbs: GET (read), POST (create), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE. The status codes come in families: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error. So when you see 404 you know the page was not found, and the fault is on the client side of the request. One more big idea: HTTP is stateless: each request stands alone, so cookies and tokens carry identity. As the figure shows, one page view is many round trips.

choices.text: The resource was not found (client error).

figures.caption: Figure 1.3.1 — loading a page
figures.note: One page view is many round trips.

keynotes: HTTP is a text protocol: a request has a method, path, headers and optional body; a response has a status code, headers and body.
Methods: GET (read), POST (create), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE; status families are 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
HTTP is stateless: each request stands alone, and cookies and tokens carry identity.

sections.title: Why latency matters
sections.body:
Why does a website feel slow even on fast internet? Because every conversation step costs a round trip, and a round trip across the sea cannot be hurried. Each trip costs the network RTT. A page needing DNS (1 RTT), TCP (1), TLS (1–2), then the request (1) needs about 4–5 RTTs before the first byte.

Do the sum. With RTT = 50 ms and four round trips (DNS, TCP, TLS, request), the time to first byte is at least 4 × 50 ms = 200 ms, before the server has even thought. HTTP/2 multiplexes requests on one connection, and HTTP/3 uses QUIC to cut handshakes. On a high-RTT link, the best way to cut page-load time is to reduce the number of round trips.

worked.why: RTT = 50 ms. Steps: DNS, TCP, TLS, request = 4 round trips.

questions.prompt: The best way to cut page-load time on a high-RTT link is…

choices.text: Fewer round trips (cache, reuse connections, bundle).

problems.prompt: RTT is 80 ms. A fresh page needs DNS, TCP, TLS (2 RTT) and the GET. Minimum time to first byte?

keynotes: Each round trip costs the network RTT; DNS (1), TCP (1), TLS (1–2) and the request (1) need about 4–5 RTTs before the first byte.
With RTT = 50 ms and four round trips, time to first byte is at least 200 ms.
HTTP/2 multiplexes requests on one connection and HTTP/3 uses QUIC to cut handshakes.

sections.title: HTML, CSS and JavaScript
sections.body:
Think of a house. The walls and rooms are the structure, the paint and furniture are the style, and the lights switching on when you clap are the behaviour. A web page has the same three layers, and you should keep them separate. HTML is structure (headings, links, forms); CSS is presentation (layout, colour); JavaScript is behaviour.

The browser parses HTML into the DOM tree and CSS into a style tree, then combines them to lay out and paint. Keep the three separate so each can change alone. If you want to change a button’s colour, that is a job for CSS.

questions.prompt: Which layer changes a button’s colour?

keynotes: HTML is structure, CSS is presentation and JavaScript is behaviour.
The browser parses HTML into the DOM tree and CSS into a style tree, then combines them to lay out and paint.
Keep the three separate so each can change alone.

sections.title: Static, dynamic and SPA
sections.body:
Not every website is built the same way, and you should know the three families. Static sites serve the same files to everyone. Dynamic sites build pages per request on the server. Single-page apps (SPAs) load one page and update it with JavaScript, fetching JSON.

Each has a trade. SPAs feel fast after the first load, but cost a heavy first load and need care for SEO. A SPA typically fetches JSON data and redraws only part of the page, rather than whole new pages.

choices.text: A full HTML page for every click.
JSON data, then updates the page in the browser.

keynotes: Static sites serve the same files to all; dynamic sites build pages per request on the server.
Single-page apps load one page and update it with JavaScript, fetching JSON.
SPAs feel fast after first load but cost a heavy first load and need care for SEO.
